title: NIC examples and the state

blocks.heading: NIC examples and the state
blocks.text: The syllabus names South Africa, India, the Philippines and Indonesia as illustrative newly industrialising countries; these are syllabus-context examples rather than a current official classification list. State provision of infrastructure, skills or enabling arrangements can support industrial capacity, but the effects depend on relevance, implementation and opportunity cost. A state can help address a missing road connection or skill shortage. It can also spend on facilities that remain unused. To evaluate its role, trace the constraint, the action and the evidence of productive or social benefit. The fictional examples here model that reasoning and are not claims that a named country used a particular policy or achieved a stated result.

blocks.heading: Evaluate an illustrative state action
blocks.text: In a fictional industrial area, firms face delivery delays and a shortage of technical skills. A freight upgrade offers earlier gains for existing firms; a training centre develops future capability but takes longer. Where delays threaten current orders, the route may merit priority. Where deliveries remain manageable but skills block expansion, training may be stronger. Compare urgency, reach, cost and longer-term benefits. This is an illustrative decision, not a claimed policy result for a named country.

blocks.heading: State roles in industrial development
blocks.text: The syllabus’s NIC examples include South Africa and India. South Africa’s public transport and electricity networks illustrate shared infrastructure used in industrial production; India’s public technical education and research illustrate support for productive skills and knowledge. Neither example proves that a single policy caused growth or that services are currently reliable. More generally a state can coordinate investment, improve export links or support access to finance. These measures have opportunity costs and can fail through poor selection or weak accountability. Test actual use, access and productive benefit rather than the spending total.
